sources.title: NASA issues long-awaited call to industry for private space stations

items.title: NASA Sets a December Deadline for Private Space Station Bids
items.body: NASA released a request to the US commercial space industry to develop private space stations that, as early as 2030, are meant to succeed the International Space Station. Industry responses are due December 8. NASA says it plans to select two or more contractors in this phase of the competition and intends to make a final decision in April.

sources.title: AI-Native Studios Can Create Original IP While Traditional Studios Keep Their Edge, VFX Veteran Hong Jae Cheol Says at Busan

items.title: AI-Native Studios Can Build Original IP, but Traditional Studios Keep the Franchises, VFX Veteran Says
items.body: At Busan, VFX veteran Hong Jae Cheol argued that small AI-native companies running automated pipelines can develop their own intellectual property, while traditional studios keep their edge in established franchises, production infrastructure, talent and distribution. Hong is a producer-director at Viscode who began his career at Industrial Light & Magic.

sources.title: Saskatoon woman transforming discarded saris, giving new purpose

items.title: Six Thousand Saris Saved From the Landfill in Saskatoon
items.body: Satya Muktinutalapati works from her house in Saskatoon turning discarded saris into new clothes. She says she has saved up to 6,000 garments from the landfill.

sources.title: ‘Between Two Lovers’ Review: Nanako Hirose’s Contentious Family Drama Examines an Ill-Fated Throuple

items.title: Nanako Hirose's 'Between Two Lovers' Builds a Family Drama Around a Throuple
items.body: The film is the sophomore feature from Nanako Hirose, a protege of Hirokazu Kore-eda. It tackles polyamorous relationships and same-sex parenting in a contemporary Japanese setting. Masami Nagasawa stars as a free-spirited children's author who invites her doting husband and secret girlfriend to enter into a three-way relationship.

sources.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London

discussion.body: The pairing of 1932 and 1937 is the quiet move here. Two eras close enough to comment on each other can do something a single period piece can't — show continuity, not just contrast.
Or it splits the attention: a play from 2013 has one centre of gravity, and spreading that across three timelines risks two of them becoming illustration for the third.

items.title: Three Gay Lives, Three Eras: 'La Bola Negra' Runs 1932, 1937 and 2017
items.body:
Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, the directors of the award-winning film La Bola Negra, used their appearance at Deadline's Contenders London to talk about the generational trauma behind it.

The structure is where that idea gets physical. The film follows the interconnected stories of three gay men in three years — 1932, 1937 and 2017 — and takes its cue from Alberto Conejero's 2013 play La piedra oscura.

Two of those years sit five years apart; the third lands eighty years later. That arrangement is a claim in itself: the 1930s and the present are put in the same frame rather than kept in separate rooms.

sources.title: Sweating the details: Sauna's potential health benefits draw scientists' interest

discussion.body: Legitimacy is a strange thing to ask for on behalf of an age-old practice. Clinical evidence isn't the only kind of value a tradition can have.
It doesn't have to be either-or. A trial can say something about what a practice does to a body without deciding what it's worth to the people who do it.

items.title: Researchers Want Rigorous Trials for Sauna and Other Heat Therapies
items.body:
A group of international researchers is pushing to rigorously study the potential health benefits of sauna and other heat therapies, NPR reports. Their stated hope is to bring scientific legitimacy to practices that are age-old.

That's a modest-sounding goal with a broad scope. "Heat therapies" reaches past the sauna, and the researchers are arguing for evidence about a whole category of treatment rather than announcing a result.

sources.title: Disappointed, angry, excited: Albertans weigh in on looming referendum

discussion.body: Annoyance that the vote is happening at all is a different political animal from a no campaign. One disputes an answer; the other disputes that there's a question worth asking.
Some of that may be timing more than conviction. People who are only starting to follow a process can sound dismissive well before they sound decided.

items.title: In Calgary, Three Moods About Alberta's Looming Referendum
items.body:
CBC News visited a library branch in Calgary to take the temperature on the referendum Alberta is heading toward. A few people there were excited to vote. Others were only just beginning to follow the process. Several said they were frustrated that Alberta was holding a referendum at all.

It's a handful of voices in one city, but the split it captures isn't yes-versus-no. Some of the feeling CBC recorded was aimed at the premise — at the fact of the vote rather than at how to cast it.

sources.title: Couples looking to have children often turn to surrogacy agencies in Georgia without understanding the hidden costs

items.title: Georgia's Surrogacy Boom Began After Russia's 2022 Invasion
items.body:
Georgia became a hub for surrogate pregnancies after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, DW reports, and the boom brought costs that aren't obvious from outside: the outlet spoke with parents and with people who hoped to become parents about what it calls the hidden costs of the industry.

A war in one country and a reproduction business expanding in another is the kind of shift that rarely shows up in headline numbers, but it shapes what individual families actually go through.

sources.title: Woman who married ISIS fighter pleads guilty to terror-related charge

items.title: Kimberly Polman Pleads Guilty to Leaving Canada for ISIS
items.body: Kimberly Polman has pleaded guilty to leaving Canada to participate in the activities of a terrorist group — the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, CBC reports. She entered the plea on Thursday. The count concerns going abroad to take part in a listed group's activities, and the plea resolves her culpability for that conduct rather than any dispute about it.

sources.title: Riyadh airport attack another dangerous moment in already tense conflict

discussion.body: Perception is the real target here. If the point of the attacks is to make Saudi Arabia look unable to protect itself, then a repaired facility and an unrepaired reputation are both results the attacker wants.

Reputation is the softer, harder-to-define half of this. Infrastructure losses are what insurers, airlines and budgets actually count; a damaged image is a judgement call that can be argued either way depending on how long the calm lasts.

items.title: The Damage a Houthi Attack Does to Saudi Arabia Is Not Only Concrete
items.body: The Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, and the BBC's reading of the current escalation draws a distinction worth keeping: the physical damage can be made good fairly quickly, while the kingdom's reputation for stability is taking the harder hit. A repair bill is finite and can be paid. A reputation for stability is a claim about the future, and the only thing that restores it is a stretch of time without further attacks. That is why campaigns that leave little structural wreckage can still be strategically costly — the target is forced to keep proving something it once could simply assume.

sources.title: In one of the country's most competitive districts, a Democrat tries to keep her seat

discussion.body: A single district is a poor measuring stick for the direction of the country. The useful figure would be how many races look like this one, and one snapshot can't supply it.

Scale aside, the shape is the interesting part. When both candidates' problems are internal, the contest becomes a test of party loyalty rather than a straight left-right argument — harder to forecast from national polling.

items.title: In a Competitive Washington Race, Both Candidates Carry a Base Problem
items.body: NPR describes a highly competitive Washington congressional race in which the incumbent Democrat has angered part of her own party's base, while the Trump-backed Republican challenger faces backlash against the party in power. The awkwardness is symmetrical: each candidate is carrying a liability generated by their own coalition rather than the opponent's. Close district races often take that shape, becoming two separate turnout problems, with the winner the one who keeps more of their own voters from staying home. Whether either camp's discontent is large enough to actually move votes is what a tight race is about to test.

sources.title: Rohan Campbell Teases Directorial Debut Plans: “A Very Personal Story”

items.title: Rohan Campbell Plans a Directorial Debut, Greenlight Pending
items.body: Rohan Campbell, whose recent work includes The Below, says he is ready to step behind the camera and intends to make his directorial debut next summer with what he calls “a very personal story.” Deadline reports he is awaiting a greenlight for it. That last detail is the operative one: a stated intention to direct and a film heading into production are different things, and only the second one lands on a release calendar.

sources.title: Oscars: U.K. Selects ‘Rehearsals for a Revolution,’ Documentary About Iran, as Best International Feature Entry

discussion.body: The vantage point is the point. A portrait of a country's turmoil made from outside it can see some things a camera inside it could not.
Distance also flattens. A country watched from far away risks becoming a single mood — turmoil as atmosphere rather than as the messy, specific thing people there actually live in.

items.title: A Film About Exile and Iran Is Already a Best Documentary Contender
items.body: Pegah Ahangarani's “Rehearsals for a Revolution” is, per IndieWire, an acclaimed look at her life in exile and at the political turmoil in her native country — and the outlet reports it was already a leading contender for Best Documentary before awards season fully gets going. That double subject is the interesting part: a personal account and a portrait of a country in crisis, carried in the same film. Exile documentaries like this one work because distance becomes method rather than limitation — the camera looks at home from a place where looking is possible.

sources.title: Brooks and Capehart on the fight for Senate control in battleground states

items.title: Three Senate Debates in One Night, and the Attacks Got Personal
items.body: Candidates for the U.S. Senate in three battleground states faced off Thursday night, in debates PBS NewsHour describes as fiery and frequently veering into personal attacks. On the broadcast, David Brooks of The Atlantic and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW joined Amna Nawaz to work through the week in politics, including the fight for control of Congress. Personal attacks are usually a measure of a race rather than of policy: the closer the contest, the less either side wants to argue on substance.

sources.title: Ukrainian prisoners of war and defectors have been gathered into a Russian battalion to face Ukrainian forces — why? And how?

items.title: Russia Says It Formed a Battalion of Ukrainian “Volunteers”
items.body: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian “volunteers,” Deutsche Welle reports. Whether that word holds is exactly the contested ground: DW reports that veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts. The label is the whole argument in miniature — a volunteer chooses, and the accounts DW describes are where that description gets tested.

sources.title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you

items.title: Boots Has Been Sold to a Canadian Billionaire Family
items.body: Boots, described by BBC Business as a stalwart of Britain's High Street, has been sold to a Canadian billionaire family. On paper it is a change of ownership, the kind of retail transaction reported in balance sheets and shareholder language. The harder question, and the one that actually touches people, is whether the shops they walk into on an ordinary afternoon change at all.

sources.title: IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit to Feature ‘Pitch Me’ Panel on Finding Breakout Hits with Top Execs and Agents

items.title: A Panel on What Buyers Look for, From Development to Acquisition
items.body: IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit, in Los Angeles on October 17, will include a panel in which key players from Independent Film Company, Gersh, Thunder Road and Madison Wells explain what they look for from development to acquisition. Two ends of one pipeline in a single session: the criteria that get a project started, and the criteria that get it bought.

sources.title: Person dies after canopy collapses at Fairmont hotel construction site

items.title: A Canopy Collapse at a Winnipeg Hotel Construction Site Kills a Worker
items.body: Global News Canada reports that a worker died after a canopy collapsed at the Fairmont Winnipeg hotel's downtown construction site on Thursday, while conducting asbestos abatement work.

sources.title: Pollo AI turns creative ideas into campaigns with OpenAI

discussion.body: The checkable part is the lineup: three named models attached to a creator tool for images and video ads. Whatever else it is, that's a clear picture of what OpenAI is pushing into creative work.
'Cinematic' is the seller's adjective, not a critic's. The sentence would read differently coming from someone who wasn't selling the software.
Fine, but a named model beats an unnamed capability. The names at least give you something to look up; the adjectives are just wrapping.

items.title: Three Model Names and a Word Like 'Cinematic'
items.body: OpenAI's customer story for Pollo AI says the tool helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads, working with GPT-5.6, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-Image-2.5. It's the vendor's own account of a customer: marketing copy that names its models.

sources.title: A life in episodes

discussion.body: Ten years of readers with competing memories is a better stress test for an autobiographical claim than the author's confidence in it. Nobody remembers alone, and the people who were there know where the seams are.

Or the past just becomes negotiable. A reader's correction is still a memory, made by someone with a stake in the version that ends up told — and the loudest correspondent isn't automatically the most accurate one.

items.title: A Memoir Serialized on Facebook, Corrected by Its Readers
items.body:
Thomas Söderqvist spent a decade posting episodes of his memoir to Facebook, and by his own account the audience did something a blank page never could: his readers corrected his understanding of his past.

The inversion is the good part. A memoir is normally a one-way claim to authority — I was there, this is how it was, trust me. Serialize it to the people who were also there, and memory becomes a draft that others can annotate. A decade is long enough for the corrections to accumulate into a running argument about a life, spread across posts.

Autobiography usually asks what you remember. This asks something harder: which parts of your own story you got wrong, and whether you can stand hearing it from the people who watched you live it.
